newsitem.title: GERMANY: UK's Rifkind warns against EMU with few members.
newsitem.headline: UK's Rifkind warns against EMU with few members.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind on Wednesday spoke against a start to Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 with only a few participants, saying it could divide the continent for decades to come.

"What the European Union is contemplating is a change that will not unite but divide its member states, against the intentions of its founding members," Rifkind told politicians, diplomats and journalists after making a speech.
"We would be embarking on a divided Europe for a whole generation," Rifkind said. "As we say in Britain, the single currency is not just for Christmas. It is forever."
Rifkind said he thought it was "unlikely" that Britain would want to join the single currency in 1999, but said the country would not take a final decision for some time.

Rifkind told journalists he did not regret using the word "hostile" to describe his government's attitude to a single European currency, but stressed he had used the word to describe Britain's position on a fudged start to the euro.
"What the government is hostile to is forcing EMU in 1999 if the convergence criteria are not met in a sustainable way and it is forced through politically," he said.

Asked if Britain would remain "hostile" to EMU if participating countries complied with the relevent criteria, Rifkind said: "If the convergence criteria were properly respected than that would ease one major area of concern."

Earlier Rifkind told BBC radio: "On balance we are hostile to a single currency, but we accept you have to think very carefully about these matters before you rule them out completely," he said. His comments sparked concern that Britain had changed its position towards the single currency, worries the finance minister Kenneth Clarke later denied.
